passage:
Dear Seema,
I need to tell someone this. Every evening I post a photo and then check the likes like a pulse. Yesterday my sketch got nine, and I felt as though I had done something wrong. Then I saw that my classmates' posts had hundreds, and I spent the whole night refreshing. My chest felt tight and I couldn't focus on chemistry.
This morning I noticed the loop: post, check, feel low, post again. So I muted three accounts that always make me feel less, and I'll only share a drawing if I still like it, not because I need a number. Can I send you my next one instead? I miss our summer evenings drawing in the courtyard 🙂
Your Leela

qa.q: How many likes did Leela's sketch get yesterday?
Why did nine likes make Leela feel so low?
qa.a: The few likes felt like a verdict on Leela's worth, bringing a low, anxious feeling and a whole night of refreshing.

qa.q: What could Leela try if the urge to check likes returns?
qa.a: Leela could remember the loop of posting, checking and feeling low, keep the accounts muted, and post only drawings Leela still likes, for personal reasons.

qa.q: How might Seema feel on receiving this letter?
qa.a: Seema may feel trusted and a little worried, and glad to be asked for the next drawing, since Leela is reaching out to a person rather than to the likes.

grounding: Shows a teen noticing the post-and-check loop of likes and choosing personal reasons to post and muting accounts.

passage:
Tuesday. Hansa posted her new dance reel at seven and checked it at 7:02, 7:05, 7:11. By bedtime it had fourteen likes. Her last one had sixty. She lay awake replaying the steps, wondering what was wrong with her. Her brother Pankaj heard her sigh through the wall.

Thursday. She was about to delete the reel and post a new one with a trending song when Pankaj leaned over. "Why are you deleting it? You loved that dance." Hansa stopped. She had loved it, on Monday, before the numbers. Now she only saw fourteen. "I keep posting, checking, feeling bad, posting again," she said slowly. "It's like a loop."

The next Monday. Hansa muted four accounts of girls whose perfect reels always made her feel clumsy. She wrote on a sticky note: "Post because I want to remember it." She danced in the living room for Pankaj and their Nani, and posted it without looking at the phone again till morning. Twenty-two likes. She noticed, then went to brush her teeth.

qa.q: How many likes did Hansa's reel have by bedtime on Tuesday?
What was Hansa feeling when she lay awake on Tuesday?
qa.a: Hansa felt low and anxious, replaying the steps and wondering what was wrong with her because of the few likes.

qa.q: What steps helped Hansa break the loop?
qa.a: Hansa named the loop, muted accounts that made her feel clumsy and wrote a reason to post that was her own.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see his sister's worry about likes?
qa.a: Pankaj seems puzzled and caring, reminding her that she loved the dance before the numbers came in.

grounding: It shows a teen who posts for likes and feels low when they are few, noticing the loop, posting for her own reasons and muting accounts that make her feel less.

passage:
Anirban, I saw your face when that photo only got a few likes. Sit with your Joseph Uncle a minute.

When I was fifteen, around 2010, there was a photo site everyone used. I'd post pictures of myself at the beach, at birthdays, with a new haircut. Then I'd refresh the page every ten minutes. If a photo didn't get at least twenty likes, I felt ugly for the whole day. I once deleted a picture of me and my grandmother because nobody liked it.

That still hurts. It was my favourite picture of her.

My older cousin told me something I didn't want to hear: "You're not posting to share. You're posting to be graded."

So I tried something. I started a small album just for myself, no posting. And I stopped following the boys whose pictures made me feel like a joke.

I'm not saying don't post, Anirban. Just ask yourself who it's for before you press the button.

qa.q: What photo did Joseph Uncle once delete?
qa.a: He deleted a picture of himself and his grandmother.

qa.q: What was young Joseph feeling when a photo got few likes?
qa.a: He felt ugly and low for the whole day, as if the likes were grading him.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Joseph break the habit, and why?
qa.a: Keeping a private album and unfollowing accounts that made him feel like a joke helped, because it let him post for his own reasons instead of for a score.

qa.q: What did the older cousin seem to feel about Joseph's posting?
qa.a: The cousin seemed worried and frank, seeing that Joseph was hurting himself by treating each post as a test.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling posting for likes and feeling low when they were few, and learning to post for his own reasons and unfollow accounts that made him feel less.
